title: Multiple dimensions of wildfire shape mammal occurrence and assemblage composition in montane eucalypt forests
content:
Mammal occurrence and assemblage composition were associated with multiple components of the fire regime, and no single wildfire history supported all species. As wildfire activity intensifies under climate change, fire and conservation management in montane forests should prioritise protecting remaining long unburnt forest, which supported a distinct mammal assemblage, and should account for variation in fire frequency, severity and time since fire across landscapes rather than managing towards a single fire history.


Abstract

Fire regimes are shifting globally, with increasing wildfire frequency and modified patterns of fire severity altering forest structure and threatening biodiversity. In south-eastern Australia's montane forests, recent decades have seen multiple wildfires occurring within short intervals and an increasing extent of high severity fire, creating uncertainty about how fauna respond to interacting fire regime components. We examined how mammal occurrence and assemblage composition respond to time since fire, fire frequency and fire severity across 68 sites spanning a range of wildfire histories in montane eucalypt forests. Sites included long unburnt forest, defined here as areas with no recorded fire since 1939, and areas burnt once, twice or three times within 20 years, at low or high severity. We used generalised linear models to assess occurrence patterns for 11 native mammal species and non-metric multidimensional scaling to evaluate assemblage composition. Mammal responses varied across fire regime dimensions, with six of 11 species associated with at least one fire variable. Long unburnt sites supported higher occurrence of dusky antechinus and eastern ringtail possums, whereas eastern pygmy-possums and common brushtail possums occurred more frequently at sites burnt in recent decades. Eastern pygmy-possum occurrence peaked at single-burn sites and was lower at double- and triple-burn sites. Long unburnt sites supported a distinct mammal assemblage relative to burnt forests. Burnt forests supported different combinations of species rather than consistent declines in occurrence across all species. Among burnt sites, assemblage composition varied along gradients of fire frequency, fire severity and time since fire, rather than forming discrete post-fire assemblages. Synthesis and applications. Mammal occurrence and assemblage composition were associated with multiple components of the fire regime, and no single wildfire history supported all species. As wildfire activity intensifies under climate change, fire and conservation management in montane forests should prioritise protecting remaining long unburnt forest, which supported a distinct mammal assemblage, and should account for variation in fire frequency, severity and time since fire across landscapes rather than managing towards a single fire history.
